public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 370

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/370](https://www.erdosproblems.com/370)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos370

/--
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that the largest prime factor of $n$ is $< n^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and
the largest prime factor of $n + 1$ is $< (n + 1)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Steinerberger has pointed out this problem has a trivial solution.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos370.lean",
formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/XC0R/formal-conjectures/blob/f58dea7d2cc5c9da2e050ec80a73e838b54a6dd2/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/370.lean#L73"]
theorem erdos_370 : answer(True) ↔
    { n | Nat.maxPrimeFac n < √n ∧ Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) < √(n + 1) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos370

review.notes: Checked the sole declaration, Erdos370.erdos_370. The source asks exactly for infinitely many n satisfying these two strict square-root bounds and records an affirmative, Lean-verified solution. The current independent problem database also records it as proved. Nat.maxPrimeFac has the intended meaning for n > 1, and Lean checks show that n = 0 and n = 1 cannot satisfy the predicate. Scratch proofs verified the coercions, equivalence with squared natural-number inequalities, and equivalence with the older supremum-based definition in the cited external proof. Computed small cases and kernel-checked that 0, 1, and 8 fail while 63 and 80 succeed. The exact independent proof compiled; its theorem depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. The formal-conjectures GitHub proof link was not opened, respecting the browsing restriction. The source's speculation that the original printed problem might contain a typo does not change the explicit question that this file faithfully states.
